nameStory: Desmodesmus protuberans gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'chain body' (desmos + desma) and Latin 'protruding' (protuberans), referring to how these tiny green algae link together in chains with bumpy projections. There isn't a widely-used common name for this microscopic organism, which is why scientists stick with the scientific name even in casual conversation.
description: **Important note: This identification is uncertain due to limited reference material.** Desmodesmus protuberans is a microscopic green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's only visible under a microscope at high magnification. These single-celled organisms form small colonies of 4-8 cells arranged in flat, chain-like groups. Each individual cell is roughly oval-shaped and contains bright green chloroplasts that help it photosynthesize like plants do. The colonies are so small they could easily fit on the point of a pin with room to spare.

funFact: Despite being invisible to our eyes, algae like Desmodesmus protuberans produce more oxygen through photosynthesis than all the world's rainforests combined - every other breath you take likely contains oxygen made by these microscopic green factories!
confusionNotes: **Confusion species uncertain due to limited reference material.** Under the microscope, it could be confused with other colonial green algae like Scenedesmus species, but Desmodesmus typically has more pronounced spines or projections on the outer cells of each colony. The chain-like arrangement and protruding features help distinguish it from round colonial algae like Volvox.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name was relatively recently split off from Scenedesmus based on genetic studies, so you might find older field guides or websites listing this species under its former name. Many microscopic algae have been reclassified in recent decades as DNA analysis reveals relationships that aren't obvious from appearance alone.
